slides.title: Chapter 12: Mining and Consensus
slides.sub: Where rewards and blocks come from, how nodes agree on one chain, and how the rules change

items.body: Picture: the Bitcoin logo, public domain (Wikimedia Commons). Python 3.14.6; Bitcoin Core 31.1 results are one recorded run, read back here.

slides.notes: This deck explains how a miner earns a reward, how every node checks and chooses blocks, how proof of work sets the pace, and how the rules of Bitcoin are changed. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library or read from one recorded run of Bitcoin Core 31.1.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.sub: Six parts; every number is a slide you can jump to

items.label: code examples with a picture of each result

slides.notes: The route has six parts that follow the order of the chapter. Four true stories and twenty-two code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
slides.take: Six parts, twenty-two examples, four true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

items: How is a block's reward made, and why can there never be more than 21 million coins?
Which checks must a transaction and a block pass before a node accepts them?
Why does a node follow the chain with the most work and not the longest?
What does a miner put into a candidate block, and what does the coinbase carry?
How do target, difficulty and retargeting set the pace of the lottery?
Why do small miners join pools, and what share of the power does an attack need?
How do hard and soft forks change the rules, and how is a soft fork voted in?

slides.notes: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.

slides.title: One chapter, six parts
slides.sub: The concept map the whole deck hangs on
slides.notes: The chapter has six parts. Together they hold 51 key concepts. Each part gets a divider, concept cards with everyday comparisons, code that runs, and some parts a true story. The deck follows the order of the chapter.
slides.take: Six parts; every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: Money and rewards
slides.sub: The reward is a wage that halves on a fixed calendar, plus tips.

items.meaning: New coins halve every 210,000 blocks, so the supply stops just below 21 million.
items.analogy: Think of a wage cut in half on a fixed calendar.

items.meaning: A block pays its miner the subsidy plus the fees of its transactions, and no more.
items.analogy: Think of a salary plus tips.

slides.notes: A miner is paid in new coins and fees. This part shows how the subsidy halves, why the supply stops just below 21 million coins, and how Core checks that a miner claims no more than the reward.

slides.title: Money and rewards: key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Halving every 210,000 blocks
items.meaning: The reward is cut in half after every 210,000 blocks, about four years.
items.analogy: Think of a wage that is halved on every fourth birthday of the system.

items.label: Total supply below 21 million
items.meaning: All rewards ever paid add up to 2,099,999,997,690,000 satoshis, just short of 21 million coins.
items.analogy: Think of a mint with a fixed stock of metal that is never topped up.

items.label: The float erratum of the book's script
items.meaning: The printed script divides with a slash, so Python 3 keeps halving fractions of a satoshi.
items.analogy: Think of a calculator that keeps cutting a coin into smaller crumbs.

items.label: Reward is subsidy plus fees
items.meaning: The miner is paid the new coins plus the fees of the included transactions.
items.analogy: Think of a wage plus tips.

items.label: The fees of block 840,000
items.meaning: The first block of the 3.125-coin era paid fees twelve times its subsidy.
items.analogy: Think of a waiter whose tips on a busy night beat the salary.

items.label: Regtest halves every 150 blocks
items.meaning: The private test chain halves the reward every 150 blocks, so a halving can be watched in minutes.
items.analogy: Think of a time-lapse film of a four-year calendar.

slides.notes: These cards cover 6 key concepts of the part Money and rewards. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 12.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Halving every 210,000 blocks
slides.sub: The reward at five heights, and the last non-zero reward

groups.note: The reward is cut in half at each multiple of 210,000 blocks, which is about every four years.
Each height becomes a subsidy in coins; the halving is a right shift of whole satoshis.
After the 33rd halving the subsidy is a single satoshi, and after the 34th it is zero.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: reward in coins from each height
The reward falls from 50 to 3.125 coins. After the 33rd halving it is 1 satoshi, and after the 34th 0.

slides.notes: The reward starts at 50 coins and is cut in half at every multiple of 210,000 blocks. The shift is done in whole satoshis, so after the 33rd halving a single satoshi is left, and after the 34th nothing. The sum of all rewards sets the supply. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The reward halves on a fixed calendar until it reaches one satoshi

slides.title: The 21 million limit
slides.sub: Whole satoshis against the book's float script

groups.note: Adding the 33 non-zero rewards, in whole satoshis, gives the real total supply.
The total falls a little short of 21 million coins, counted in satoshis.
The book's script divides with a slash, which Python 3 turns into a float division.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the supply, in whole satoshis
The exact total is 2,099,999,997,690,000 satoshis. Run as printed, the book's script ends with a float, which hides the shortfall.

slides.notes: Adding the 33 non-zero rewards in whole satoshis gives a total just below 21 million coins. The book's script divides with a slash, which in Python 3 is a float division. Run as printed it ends at a float and never shows the shortfall. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The real total is a little under 21 million coins, and a float hides that

slides.title: Subsidy plus fees is the reward
slides.sub: A private chain: what Core offers and what a miner claims

groups.note: Bitcoin Core, on a private chain, offers a block template that states the reward.
The reward it offers equals the subsidy plus the fees of the chosen transactions.
A miner may claim less than the reward, but one satoshi more is refused.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: satoshis offered and claimed
Subsidy plus fees equals the reward: yes. The claim is one satoshi less and is accepted; one more gives bad-cb-amount.

slides.notes: Bitcoin Core offered a reward made of the subsidy and the fees of the chosen transactions. A miner claimed one satoshi less and the block was accepted. A test block that claimed one satoshi more was refused with the name bad-cb-amount. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A miner may claim less than the reward, never one satoshi more

slides.title: Tips twelve times the wage
slides.sub: The subsidy halves on schedule, but fees can swing wildly

items.cap: Antminer ASIC Miner - Steve Rainwater, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: Block 840,000, mined by ViaBTC at 00:09:27 UTC on 20 April 2024, was the first to pay the new subsidy of 3.125 coins.
WHY: Its 3,050 transactions paid 3,762,561,499 satoshis in fees, 12.04 times the subsidy, so the reward was mostly tips.
HOW: The sum was recomputed from the saved block; its coinbase carries the tag ViaBTC, by which pool statistics are made.
SO WHAT: The book says that fees are a small part of income; this block is an exception.

items.body: Stand-in picture: a mining machine, not block 840,000

items.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, who wrote the halving schedule, and ViaBTC, the pool that mined block 840,000
items.where: the main chain of Bitcoin, block 840,000, as listed by mempool.space

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2024-04-20. Block 840,000 was mined at 00:09:27 UTC on 20 April 2024 and was the first to pay the new subsidy of 3.125 coins, half of 6.25. The lesson is that the subsidy halves on schedule, but fees can swing wildly.

slides.title: Verifying and agreeing
slides.sub: Every node is a customs officer who checks each parcel against the same list.

items.meaning: Every node tests every transaction and block against the same list of rules.
items.analogy: Think of a customs officer with a printed checklist.

items.meaning: Nodes follow the chain with the most accumulated work, not the one with most blocks.
items.analogy: Think of the heaviest rope, not the longest.

slides.notes: No one is in charge, so every node checks everything itself. We run the rules for transactions and blocks, and see why the chain with the most work wins, not the longest chain.

slides.title: Verifying and agreeing: key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Transaction checklist
items.meaning: Each transaction is tested against fixed rules and refused with a named reason.
items.analogy: Think of a customs officer with a printed checklist.

items.label: Block checklist
items.meaning: Each block must also obey the rules of reward, height, merkle root, time and version.
items.analogy: Think of an exam paper marked against a model answer.

items.label: Coinbase maturity
items.meaning: A mining reward can be spent only after 100 confirmations.
items.analogy: Think of a cheque that clears only after a hundred days.

items.label: Most work, not longest
items.meaning: Nodes follow the chain with the most accumulated work, not the one with the most blocks.
items.analogy: Think of the heaviest rope, not the longest rope.

slides.notes: These cards cover Transaction checklist, Block checklist, Coinbase maturity and Most work, not longest. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 12.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A transaction faces a checklist
slides.sub: Spoiled transactions and the reasons Core gave

groups.note: Bitcoin Core, on a private chain, was asked to test several spoiled transactions.
Each broken rule gets a name; a coinbase may be spent only after 100 confirmations.
With 100 confirmations the same spend is allowed.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: named reasons from Bitcoin Core
Each refusal names the rule it broke. Only the coinbase at depth 100 is allowed.

slides.notes: Each node tests every transaction against the same rules. We asked a private node about a spoiled transaction and got a named reason each time. A coinbase output is refused at depth 99 and accepted at depth 100. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Every refusal has a name, and a fresh coinbase cannot be spent before 100 blocks

slides.title: A block faces its own checklist
slides.sub: Fourteen test blocks, each breaking one rule

groups.note: The same node was given blocks that each broke exactly one rule.
Each broken rule answers with a short reason; the valid block is accepted.
The reasons name the rule: the reward, the height, the merkle root and the clock.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: six of the 14 test blocks
The valid block is accepted; every other block is refused with a name for its rule.

slides.notes: The block checks go further than the transaction checks. We handed Core blocks that each broke one rule. The reward one satoshi too high, a missing height, a wrong merkle root, a wrong clock or an old version each got its own named reason. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Reward, height, merkle root, clock and version each have a rule of their own

slides.title: The best chain has the most work
slides.sub: Two branches on a private chain, and a reversed payment

groups.note: Two competing branches were built on a private chain; the first had paid Carol.
The chain work of each tip is a number; the larger number wins, not the longer chain.
After the switch the payment has fewer confirmations than before, and Carol holds nothing.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: chain work of the two tips
The second branch has more work, so it wins: yes. Carol held 49.999 before and 0.0 after; the payment went from 1 to -2 confirmations.

slides.notes: Two branches were built, and the first paid Carol. The second branch carried more chain work, so Core switched to it and the payment fell out of the chain. This is why a shop waits for confirmations. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A heavier branch replaces a lighter one, even when both have equal length

slides.title: Building the block
slides.sub: The miner packs a parcel and writes the label before sealing it.

items.meaning: A node picks transactions by fee rate up to a weight limit.
items.analogy: Think of a loader who packs the best-paying parcels first.

items.meaning: The first transaction creates the reward and carries the height and a witness commitment.
items.analogy: Think of the first line of a ledger, with no payer.

items.meaning: Six fields in 80 bytes, with a time that must pass two rules.
items.analogy: Think of the address label on the parcel.

slides.notes: Before the lottery starts the miner builds a candidate block. We read the coinbase that Core makes today, take an 80-byte header apart, and see how the extra nonce gives a new search space.

slides.title: Building the block: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Block template
items.meaning: A node offers a template with transactions picked by fee rate, up to a weight limit.
items.analogy: Think of a loader who packs the best-paying parcels first.

items.label: Coinbase fields of Bitcoin Core today
items.meaning: Core 31.1 fills in the lock time, the sequence and the end of the script in ways the book's table does not show.
items.analogy: Think of a form that the clerk now fills in for you.

items.label: Coinbase data and tags
items.meaning: The free bytes of the coinbase script, two to one hundred in all, are where pools sign their blocks.
items.analogy: Think of the baker's mark pressed into each loaf.

items.label: BIP 34 height push
items.meaning: The coinbase script starts with the block height, so every coinbase differs.
items.analogy: Think of the page number written on the first line of each page.

items.label: Witness commitment
items.meaning: An extra coinbase output commits to the witness data of all transactions.
items.analogy: Think of a sealed envelope that lists what lies in the second drawer.

items.label: The extra nonce space
items.meaning: Eight extra bytes in the coinbase script give a miner 2 to the 96 headers to try.
items.analogy: Think of a second, far larger drum behind the lottery drum.

slides.notes: These cards cover Block template, Coinbase fields of Bitcoin Core today, Coinbase data and tags, BIP 34 height push, Witness commitment and The extra nonce space. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 12.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: The coinbase of Bitcoin Core today
slides.sub: Height, lock time and sequence in the first transaction

groups.note: Bitcoin Core builds a block template; its weight limit leaves room for the header.
The coinbase script starts with the block height as a short pushed number.
Other fields are set by Core, not by the book: the lock time and the sequence.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the first transaction of a Core block
The script is the height as a short push, 029c08, and a zero byte. Core sets version 2.

slides.notes: The coinbase script starts with the block height as a short pushed number. Bitcoin Core 31.1 also sets the lock time to the height minus one and a sequence below the maximum. The template's weight limit leaves room for the block header. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Core sets the lock time and the sequence, which the book does not say

slides.title: Building the block: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: The extra nonce changes the root
items.meaning: A counter in the coinbase script changes the merkle root and so opens a fresh search space.
items.analogy: Think of reshuffling the deck before the next draw.

items.label: Median time past
items.meaning: A block's time must be later than the median of the last eleven blocks.
items.analogy: Think of a clock that follows the majority, not a single watch.

items.label: Two-hour rule
items.meaning: A block time more than two hours ahead of a node's clock is refused.
items.analogy: Think of a rule against post-dated cheques.

slides.notes: These cards cover The extra nonce changes the root, Median time past and Two-hour rule. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 12.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: The header of a mined block
slides.sub: Eighty bytes, and a hash under the target

groups.note: The 80-byte header of a regtest block is taken apart into its six fields.
The hash of the header must not be larger than the target that its bits describe.
Regtest has a huge target, so one zero bit of hash is enough.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: a regtest header taken apart
The bits 207fffff describe a huge target, so 6 zero bits are enough on this private chain.

slides.notes: The header of a regtest block is eighty bytes with six fields. Its hash, read as a number, is not larger than the target that the bits describe. On regtest the target is huge, so a few zero bits are enough. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A valid header hashes to a number that is not above its target

slides.title: A new extra nonce, a new root
slides.sub: Same block, one counter changed in the coinbase

groups.note: A miner built the same block twice, changing only a counter in the coinbase script.
The coinbase transaction id differs, so the merkle root differs as well.
The nonce in the header is the same in both, but the header hash is not.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: the same block, two extra nonces
Only the counter in the coinbase changed, yet the header is new.

slides.notes: A miner that has used up the nonce changes a counter in the coinbase script. That changes the coinbase id, the merkle root and so the whole header. The header's own nonce can start again from zero. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The header's nonce stays, yet the hash is new: a fresh search space

slides.title: Proof of work
slides.sub: Proof of work is a lottery whose tickets are costly to draw and cheap to check.

items.meaning: Try numbers until the hash falls under the target; checking takes one hash.
items.analogy: Think of rolling dice until a six.

items.meaning: A four-byte code holds the target; difficulty says how small it is.
items.analogy: Think of the height of a limbo bar.

items.meaning: Every 2,016 blocks the target is scaled so blocks keep coming every ten minutes.
items.analogy: Think of a thermostat for the pace of the lottery.

slides.notes: Proof of work is a lottery with a target. We play it with a text, read the target from the bits, turn difficulty into days, and follow the retarget rule on a real period of 2024.

slides.title: Proof of work: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: The Hello World nonce
items.meaning: Hash a text with a counter added, again and again, until the hash starts with zeros.
items.analogy: Think of rolling a die until a six turns up.

items.label: Proof is cheap to check
items.meaning: Finding a valid header takes billions of hashes, and checking it takes one.
items.analogy: Think of a jigsaw piece: hard to find, easy to see that it fits.

items.label: Hash below target
items.meaning: A header is valid when its hash, read as a number, is not above the target.
items.analogy: Think of a limbo bar that the hash must pass under.

items.label: Compact bits
items.meaning: The target is stored in four bytes: one for the size and three for the digits.
items.analogy: Think of scientific notation for a huge number.

items.label: The wait of a terahash miner
items.meaning: At the difficulty of block 277,316 a miner doing one terahash a second waited about 59 days.
items.analogy: Think of one person with a single ticket in a national lottery.

items.label: Hash rate from difficulty
items.meaning: Difficulty times 2 to the 32, over 600 seconds, estimates the hashes a second of the network.
items.analogy: Think of guessing the size of a crowd from the effort needed to get in.

slides.notes: These cards cover The Hello World nonce, Proof is cheap to check, Hash below target, Compact bits, The wait of a terahash miner and Hash rate from difficulty. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 12.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Proof of work is a nonce lottery
slides.sub: Hello, world! with a counter, and the tries for each zero

groups.note: A small w gives the book's hash; the capital W it types gives another.

rows: ok = lambda n, z: hw(n).startswith('0' * z)
f = lambda z: next(n for n in ns if ok(n, z))
groups.note: A try counts if the hash starts with z zero digits.
Tries needed for one, two, three and four zero digits.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library, R its regtest record

items.body: Result: tries until the hash starts with zeros
The book prints the hash 09cb91f8 for the capital W, but that is the hash of the small w. The capital W gives 6bbe6a3d.

slides.notes: The book hashes a text with a counter added. The first hash that starts with a zero comes at counter 32. Every further zero digit makes the search about sixteen times longer, while checking the answer always takes a single hash. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Each extra zero digit costs about sixteen times more tries

slides.title: The stamp that made email cost
slides.sub: Proof of work was invented to price email, years before Bitcoin

items.cap: Adam Back - Joi Ito, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: Adam Back proposed Hashcash in 1997 and wrote it up in a paper dated 1 August 2002: a stamp of computing work that makes sending mail cost a little.
WHY: Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor had proposed in 1992 to price junk mail with a moderately hard function; Hashcash made the idea practical.
HOW: The sender hashes a string with a growing counter until the hash starts with zeros, as in our lottery; the receiver checks it with one hash.
SO WHAT: Satoshi Nakamoto's paper of 2008 calls Bitcoin's proof of work similar to Adam Back's Hashcash.

items.who: Adam Back, the cryptographer who proposed Hashcash, Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor, who proposed pricing functions against junk mail
items.where: the paper Hashcash - A Denial of Service Counter-Measure, dated 1 August 2002, and the Bitcoin paper of 2008

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2002-08-01. Proof of work did not start with Bitcoin: Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor proposed in 1992 that a user should compute a moderately hard function before using a shared resource, to fight junk mail. The lesson is that a cheap check of an expensive search can price any request.

slides.title: Proof of work: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: The 2015-gap retarget
items.meaning: 2,016 blocks have only 2,015 gaps, and the rule measures the span from the first block to the last.
items.analogy: Think of counting fence posts and the spaces between them.

items.label: The factor-of-four clamp
items.meaning: One retarget never moves the target by more than a factor of four either way.
items.analogy: Think of a speed limiter on the steering wheel.

items.label: The BIP 94 branch
items.meaning: Testnet4 measures the period from its first block, so a late block cannot trick the rule.
items.analogy: Think of a stopwatch started at the start line.

items.label: Regtest never retargets
items.meaning: A chain parameter switches the difficulty adjustment off, so the difficulty of regtest stays the same.
items.analogy: Think of a thermostat that has been unplugged.

slides.sub: Block 277,316 as the book lists it

slides.sub: A period far too fast, on time, and far too slow

slides.title: Competition and attacks
slides.sub: Mining is a race of lottery syndicates, and a big syndicate may cheat.

items.meaning: Four billion tries are used up at once, so miners vary other fields too.
items.analogy: Think of a combination lock with too few wheels.

items.meaning: Small miners pool power and share the pay, at the price of trust.
items.analogy: Think of a lottery syndicate that splits small wins.

items.meaning: A share of the power buys odds of rewriting recent history.
items.analogy: Think of a runner chasing a leader.

slides.notes: Mining is a race. The nonce space runs out, small miners form pools, and a large share of the power buys the odds of an attack. We compute each of these.

slides.title: Competition and attacks: concepts (1 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: The nonce space is tiny
items.meaning: 32 bits give 4.3 billion tries, which a modern machine uses up in a fraction of a second.
items.analogy: Think of a padlock with only a few wheels.

items.label: Version rolling
items.meaning: 16 bits of the version field may be changed freely, which multiplies the search space.
items.analogy: Think of a spare dial on the lock.

items.label: Covert ASICBoost
items.meaning: A way of building the block header so that mining hardware does less work per hash.
items.analogy: Think of a baker who reuses one batch of dough for many loaves.

items.label: Pool shares and fees
items.meaning: A pool pays members for easy partial solutions and keeps a fee.
items.analogy: Think of a lottery syndicate that splits small wins.

items.label: Stratum protocols
items.meaning: The language a pool and a mining machine speak, in use since 2012 and followed by a second version.
items.analogy: Think of the radio code between a dispatcher and a taxi.

items.label: Solo miner variance
items.meaning: A small miner may wait years for one block, so income is very uneven.
items.analogy: Think of fishing alone in a very large lake.

slides.notes: These cards cover The nonce space is tiny, Version rolling, Covert ASICBoost, Pool shares and fees, Stratum protocols and Solo miner variance. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 12.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.sub: How often the nonce space is emptied each second

groups.note: The hash rate of 15 October 2026, typed from the saved figure, in hashes a second.
A miner could empty the 32-bit nonce this many times in every second.

slides.title: Competition and attacks: concepts (2 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Block withholding
items.meaning: A pool member who hides a full solution harms the pool and not the member.
items.analogy: Think of a saboteur on a team who pockets the winning ticket.

items.label: Nakamoto's catch-up odds
items.meaning: The chance that an attacker catches up falls quickly with the number of blocks behind.
items.analogy: Think of a runner who starts further behind each time.

items.label: The selfish-mining threshold
items.meaning: Above a share between one quarter and one third, hiding blocks can pay.
items.analogy: Think of a card player who holds back a winning card.

slides.title: Changing the rules
slides.sub: Changing the rules is repainting the road signs while cars still drive.

items.meaning: Looser rules split the chain into two histories.
items.analogy: Think of a road that forks, with no way back.

items.meaning: Stricter rules stay valid for old nodes and are switched on by a vote.
items.analogy: Think of a stricter door policy.

slides.notes: Rules change by forks. We watch a looser and a stricter node disagree, time a minority chain, follow a BIP 9 vote and read the heights of old soft forks in the source code.

slides.title: Changing the rules: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: A soft fork only tightens
items.meaning: The new rules are a subset of the old, so old nodes still accept the new blocks.
items.analogy: Think of a stricter door policy that the old doorman still accepts.

items.label: The minority chain is slow
items.meaning: A branch with a small share of the power keeps the old difficulty and runs slowly.
items.analogy: Think of a bus timetable kept after most buses left.

items.label: The chain split of March 2013
items.meaning: A large block was valid for new nodes and refused by old ones, and the chain split for hours.
items.analogy: Think of two dictionaries that disagree on one word.

items.label: The Bitcoin Cash fork of 2017
items.meaning: A group changed the rules so that its blocks were refused by the old network, and a second coin was born.
items.analogy: Think of a village that splits in two but keeps one history.

items.label: BIP 34 activation
items.meaning: The first soft fork switched on by counting block versions: 750, then 950, of the last 1,000 blocks.
items.analogy: Think of a show of hands among the last thousand voters.

items.label: The BIP 9 state machine
items.meaning: A deployment moves from defined through started and locked in to active as miners signal.
items.analogy: Think of a traffic light that changes in a fixed order.

slides.notes: These cards cover 6 key concepts of the part Changing the rules. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 12.

slides.sub: A loose and a strict node on a private chain

The loose node accepts a block with no height; the strict node refuses it.
The loose chain goes on, the strict node follows only blocks that obey: the two tips differ.

The two nodes now follow different chains: the chain has split.

slides.title: Hard fork or soft fork?
slides.sub: Why one splits the chain and the other does not

left.head: A hard fork loosens the rules
rows: New blocks may break the old rules.
Old nodes refuse them, and the chain splits.
Like a fork in the road.

right.head: A soft fork tightens the rules
rows: New blocks still obey the old rules.
Old nodes accept them, and the chain stays whole.

slides.notes: A hard fork loosens the rules, so old nodes refuse the new blocks and two histories grow. A soft fork tightens them, so old nodes still accept every new block. A soft fork needs a majority of the miners, but not of the nodes.
slides.take: A soft fork needs most of the miners; a hard fork needs everyone

slides.title: Changing the rules: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: BIP 8 lock-in by height
items.meaning: It counts in block heights, not time, and can force the lock-in when the timeout comes.
items.analogy: Think of a deadline set by page number, not by the clock.

items.label: Segwit activation in 2017
items.meaning: Miners held it back under BIP 9 until BIP 91 and BIP 148; it became active on 24 August 2017.
items.analogy: Think of a vote that stalled until everyone was given a deadline.

items.label: Speedy Trial and taproot
items.meaning: A three-month vote that needed 90 percent, then a delay before the new rules began.
items.analogy: Think of a short referendum with a high bar.

items.label: Buried deployments
items.meaning: Old soft forks are now plain activation heights in the source code.
items.analogy: Think of a law so old that it is printed in the constitution.

items.label: BIP 54 consensus cleanup
items.meaning: A proposal that would fix the time warp attack and limit signature operations and transaction size.
items.analogy: Think of a spring clean of an old rulebook.

slides.title: The day Bitcoin had two histories
slides.sub: An accident in software became a rule of the network

items.cap: Fork in the road - Ian Sane, CC BY 2.0, Flickr

items: WHAT: On 11 March 2013 block 225,430 was valid for Bitcoin 0.8 and refused by older nodes, so the chain split for 24 blocks, about six hours.
WHY: Older versions had too few Berkeley DB locks for a large block, and this accident had become a rule of consensus.
HOW: Marek Palatinus and Michael Marsee moved their pools back to 0.7, so the old chain carried the most work; Gavin Andresen wrote BIP 50.
SO WHAT: Most large businesses paused deposits: they knew that the chain with the most work wins.

items.body: Stand-in picture: a fork in a road stands for the split

items.who: Gavin Andresen, who wrote the post-mortem BIP 50, Marek Palatinus (Slush) and Michael Marsee (Eleuthria of BTCGuild)
items.where: the Bitcoin network, from block 225,430, and BIP 50 in the bitcoin/bips repository

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2013-03-11. On 11 March 2013 at 23:24:19 UTC block 225,430, with 797 transactions, was mined and accepted by nodes of Bitcoin 0.8 but rejected by some older nodes. The lesson is that an accident in software can become a rule of the network.

slides.title: A ninety percent vote on a clock
slides.sub: Fail fast or succeed: a short vote keeps a soft fork calm

items.cap: Taproot profile - Forest and Kim Starr, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: Taproot was activated by Speedy Trial: it opened on 24 April 2021, timed out on 11 August 2021 and needed 1,815 of 2,016 blocks.
WHY: A short vote at 90 percent makes a soft fork succeed or fail quickly, and a minimum activation height gave nodes time to upgrade.
HOW: F2Pool mined block 709,632 on 14 November 2021 with version 0x20200004, in which bit 2 is the taproot signal.
SO WHAT: Bitcoin Core 31.1 still holds these parameters in chainparams.cpp, which is how the dates were recomputed.

items.body: Stand-in picture: a taproot stands for the name

items.who: Pieter Wuille, Jonas Nick and Anthony Towns, the authors of BIP 341, and F2Pool, which mined the first block under the new rules
items.where: the main chain of Bitcoin at block 709,632, and BIP 341 in the bitcoin/bips repository

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2021-11-14. Taproot was activated by a variant of BIP 9 called Speedy Trial, which opened on 24 April 2021, timed out on 11 August 2021 and needed 1,815 of 2,016 blocks, 90 percent, instead of 1,916. The lesson is that fail fast or succeed: a short vote keeps a soft fork calm.

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.sub: One line per idea, each provable from its slides

items: The reward is subsidy plus fees; the subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks, and the supply stops just below 21 million coins.
Every node checks every transaction and block by the same rules, and follows the chain with the most work.
A candidate block has a template, a coinbase with the height, and a header whose nonce, extra nonce and version are searched.
Proof of work is a hash below a target; retargeting every 2,016 blocks keeps the pace at ten minutes, at most fourfold per step.
Pools smooth a miner's income, attacks need a large share, and soft forks tighten the rules by a vote.

slides.notes: These five lines are the deck in miniature. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was computed there. The chapter code tab of the course page reruns all twenty-two examples.
slides.take: If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part carries the receipt
